> **How to read this file.** Section 3 runs the simulation, sections 4 and 5 show the evidence, and section 8 states my selected n. The reusable code lives in `R/functions.R`; this file only calls it.

## 1. Prediction

> The population is already normal. I predict the sample mean is exactly normal at **every** n, even n = 1, and that its spread shrinks like 1/√n. For example, at n = 10 I expect the SD of the sample means to be about 1 √10 ≈ 0.316, and skewness and kurtosis to be near 0 at every n. This serves as a control so I can compare it to other distributions that may not be normal at a given n.

## 2. The population

```{r}
#| label: setup
source("R/setup.R")
source("R/functions.R")

generator <- function(n) rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
mu    <- 0
sigma <- 1
```

Standard Normal: mean μ = 0, standard deviation σ = 1, so the theoretical standard error of the mean is SE = σ/√n = 1/√n.

```{r}
#| label: population-plot
#| fig-height: 3
curve(dnorm(x), from = -4, to = 4, lwd = 3, col = "steelblue",
      main = "Standard Normal population", xlab = "x", ylab = "density")
```

## 3. Simulation

For every sample size n in my list (`r min(n_values)` to `r max(n_values)`, `r length(n_values)` sizes), I draw B = `r format(B, big.mark = ",")` samples of n observations and keep each sample's mean. B is the number of repetitions; n is the size of each sample.

```{r}
#| label: simulate
all_means <- simulate_all_n(generator, n_values)
results   <- summarize_means(all_means, mu, sigma)
results$good <- flag_good(results)

dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE)
write.csv(results, "results/01_normal.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

## 4. Results

Selected sample sizes (the full table of all `r nrow(results)` sizes is saved in `results/01_normal.csv`):

```{r}
#| label: table
key_n <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 100)
show  <- results[results$n %in% key_n, c("n", "sim_mean", "theory_mean", "sim_sd",
                                         "theory_se", "sd_ratio", "skewness",
                                         "excess_kurtosis")]
show$passes <- ifelse(results$good[results$n %in% key_n], "yes", "no")
knitr::kable(show, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

Note: These four sample sizes are a sample of the picture: 1 is the raw population, 2 is the smallest amount of averaging, 5 is a small sample, and 30 is the classic rule of thumb. Every n from 1 to 100 appears in the diagnostics chart below and in `results/01_normal.csv`, and you can watch any n live in the **Interactive Sampling Distribution Explorer**

## 5. Plots

**Histograms of the sample means**, with the theoretical normal curve N(μ, σ/√n) in red:

```{r}
#| label: histograms
plot_histograms(all_means, c(1, 2, 5, 30), mu, sigma, "Standard Normal")
```

**Q–Q plots** (points on the red line = normal):

```{r}
#| label: qqplots
plot_qq(all_means, c(1, 2, 5, 30), "Standard Normal")
```

**Diagnostics across every n.** Dashed lines mark my "good enough" limits (defined in section 6):

```{r}
#| label: diagnostics
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
plot(results$n, results$skewness, type = "b", pch = 16, cex = 0.6,
     ylim = range(c(results$skewness, -0.25, 0.25)),
     xlab = "n", ylab = "skewness", main = "Skewness of sample means")
abline(h = c(-0.25, 0, 0.25), lty = c(2, 1, 2), col = "firebrick")

plot(results$n, results$excess_kurtosis, type = "b", pch = 16, cex = 0.6,
     ylim = range(c(results$excess_kurtosis, -0.5, 0.5)),
     xlab = "n", ylab = "excess kurtosis", main = "Excess kurtosis")
abline(h = c(-0.5, 0, 0.5), lty = c(2, 1, 2), col = "firebrick")

plot(results$n, results$sd_ratio, type = "b", pch = 16, cex = 0.6,
     ylim = range(c(results$sd_ratio, 0.95, 1.05)),
     xlab = "n", ylab = "simulated SD / theoretical SE", main = "Spread vs. theory")
abline(h = c(0.95, 1, 1.05), lty = c(2, 1, 2), col = "firebrick")
```

## 6. My definition of "approximately normal"

For a sample size n to count as approximately normal, I require **all** of the following:

1.  The histogram is bell-shaped and the Q–Q plot is close to the line.
2.  \|skewness\| ≤ 0.25.
3.  \|excess kurtosis\| ≤ 0.5.
4.  The simulated SD is within 5% of the theoretical SE (σ/√n).

My selected n is the smallest n that passes and stays passing for every larger n I tested, so a lucky pass at one n doesn't count.

**Why these cutoffs.**

| Check | Cutoff | Why this number |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| Skewness | ±0.25 | A common rule of thumb calls \|skewness\| \< 0.5 "approximately symmetric," and I use half of that. At 0.25, a normal-based 95% interval puts about 1.8% in one tail and 3.1% in the other instead of 2.5% each (checked with the exact Gamma distribution of the Exponential mean at n = 64). That is a visible but modest error. |
| Excess kurtosis | ±0.5 | This is the tail weight of a t distribution with 16 degrees of freedom, whose 97.5% point is 2.12 versus 1.96 for the normal. That is already close to normal. |
| SD vs. theory | within 5% | If the true SD is 5% off, an interval that claims 95% actually covers between 93.8% and 96.1%. |

**Note**: This is my interpretation. A stricter or looser rule would change the selected n, which is why I state the rule openly and use it the same way in every analysis.

## 7. Interpretation

```{r}
#| label: n-star
n_star     <- smallest_good_n(results)
max_skew   <- max(abs(results$skewness))
max_kurt   <- max(abs(results$excess_kurtosis))
sd_lo      <- min(results$sd_ratio)
sd_hi      <- max(results$sd_ratio)
max_mean_err <- max(abs(results$sim_mean - results$theory_mean))
```

- **Shape.** The histograms and Q–Q plots look normal at every n shown, including n = 1. That makes sense: the average of normal observations is exactly normal, so the CLT is not needed here.
- **Mean.** The simulated mean never differs from μ = 0 by more than `r round(max_mean_err, 3)`.
- **Spread.** The simulated SD divides by the theoretical SE to between `r round(sd_lo, 3)` and `r round(sd_hi, 3)`, so the formula σ/√n holds for every n.
- **Skewness and kurtosis.** Across all `r nrow(results)` sizes, \|skewness\| never exceeds `r round(max_skew, 3)` and \|excess kurtosis\| never exceeds `r round(max_kurt, 3)`. These are not real non-normality; they are **simulation noise** from using `r format(B, big.mark = ",")` repetitions. So in the other populations I will treat skewness within about ±`r round(max_skew, 2)` and excess kurtosis within about ±`r round(max_kurt, 2)` as "basically zero."

**CLT assumptions.** Observations are independent, identically distributed, and have finite variance, so every assumption is met.

**Limitations / surprises.** The only wiggle in the results is random noise, and it is small. A different seed would shift those small wiggles a little, not the conclusion.

## 8. Selected n and justification

**Selected n = `r n_star`.**

The sampling distribution of the mean is normal already at n = 1, and it passes all four of my criteria at every sample size I tested (n = `r min(n_values)` to `r max(n_values)`). So for a Normal population the answer to "how big must n be?" is that there is no minimum, and the number 30 plays no role.
